paragraphs: Many learning systems contain hidden choices between discrete categories, such as actions, graph connections, or latent classes. These choices are difficult to train with gradient descent. This paper addresses the problem by changing how category probabilities are represented, complementing research that improves estimates of the gradients themselves.

The proposed function, catnat, constructs categorical probabilities through a hierarchy of binary splits. The authors analyze this representation using information geometry, which describes how changes in model parameters affect probability distributions. They prove that catnat produces a diagonal Fisher Information Matrix and establish advantages for gradient descent. This gives the proposed replacement a mathematical rationale beyond an empirical comparison with softmax.

Experiments covering graph structure learning, variational autoencoders, and reinforcement learning report more efficient learning and consistently better test performance. The authors also describe catnat as straightforward to implement and compatible with standard training stabilization methods. The contribution therefore combines a different probability representation, theoretical support for its optimization properties, and evidence of benefits across several tested applications.
icml-2026-beyond-softmax-a-natural-param.tldr: Catnat represents categorical probabilities through hierarchical binary choices, with theoretical optimization advantages and improved learning in several applications.

paragraphs: Turning a spoken request into a tool call requires both understanding speech and selecting the correct operation and arguments. Similar-sounding words, background noise, and interrupted speech can change crucial details. Conversations may also require clarification before a tool can be called. BFCL Audio builds an evaluation around these combined demands.

The benchmark contains 6,200 expert-verified tasks in two suites. One evaluates systems that transcribe speech before sending text to a language model; the other evaluates systems that accept audio and produce tool calls directly. A controllable audio pipeline introduces variations in accent, speaking speed, disfluencies, and noise, allowing speech conditions to be examined systematically.

Automatic grading checks function names and argument values through structural matching for single-turn calls and response or state measures for multi-turn interactions. This supports evaluation without language-model judges. The authors test a broad collection of models, organize failures into a taxonomy, and analyze which speech factors affect accuracy most. The released benchmark, grading tools, and audio pipeline provide infrastructure for studying reliability across both deployment styles.
icml-2026-bfcl-audio-an-audio-function-c.tldr: BFCL Audio evaluates how reliably speech-based agents turn spoken requests into correct tool calls under varied conversational and acoustic conditions.

paragraphs: Human demonstrations can show what a manipulated object should do, but robot hands have different physical capabilities. DexMachina studies how to learn robot policies that reproduce demonstrated object states. Its focus is extended tasks involving two hands and articulated objects, where many possible actions and discontinuities in motion and contact complicate learning.

The method introduces a curriculum built around virtual object controllers. Initially, these controllers automatically move the object toward its target states, providing motion and contact guidance while the policy learns. Their strength then decreases, allowing the robot policy to gradually take responsibility for the manipulation. The central idea is to make the desired object behavior available during training while progressively removing assistance.

The authors release a simulation benchmark spanning multiple tasks and dexterous hand designs, and report substantial improvements over baseline methods. Because success is assessed through object manipulation, the framework also supports functional comparisons between hardware designs. Quantitative and qualitative results inform these comparisons, positioning the benchmark as a platform for studying which hand capabilities support useful manipulation.
icml-2026-dexmachina-functional-retarget.tldr: DexMachina teaches two-handed robot manipulation by gradually withdrawing virtual assistance that guides objects through demonstrated target states.

paragraphs: An explanation can sound convincing without helping someone predict what a model will actually do. This paper makes that predictive usefulness the training target. Its explanation model, OPeX, aims to describe observable input–output behavior faithfully, addressing the gap between plausible rationales and explanations that track the model being explained.

OPeX uses reinforcement learning with Group Relative Policy Optimization to optimize two complementary measures. Recoverability asks whether an explanation lets a reader or system reconstruct predictions on examples already seen. Simulatability asks whether it supports predicting the model’s responses to new inputs. Together, these measures reward explanations that capture both existing decisions and behavior beyond the examples used to illustrate them.

Across structured and text tasks, the authors report approximately 0.99 recoverability and 0.85 simulatability using an 8-billion-parameter backbone. OPeX outperforms the listed language-model, explanation-method, and human-written alternatives. Human studies also report a 15% improvement in classification accuracy over competent baselines. These findings support directly training explanations for behavioral prediction rather than relying on their apparent plausibility.
icml-2026-directly-optimizing-natural-la.tldr: OPeX trains natural-language explanations to recover known model decisions and predict unseen ones, improving behavioral faithfulness and human classification performance.

paragraphs: Preference-based fine-tuning can lose effectiveness when deployment prompts differ substantially from the prompts represented in training feedback. This paper develops robust training methods intended to preserve performance under that distribution shift. The problem is therefore about how well learned preferences transfer to different downstream tasks.

The authors formulate distributionally robust versions of two approaches: reward-based reinforcement learning from human feedback and direct preference optimization, which does not require a separate reward model. They propose minibatch gradient-descent algorithms for both formulations and prove convergence guarantees. The framework brings robustness to both learning through an explicit reward signal and optimizing a policy directly from preferences.

The evaluation trains on Unified-Feedback and tests on two other datasets. Robust training improves reward-model accuracy on average, with particularly marked gains on some tasks, including reasoning. Robust policy optimization also improves performance on the tested out-of-distribution tasks. These results provide empirical evidence that accounting for prompt-distribution changes during training can help both preference assessment and the resulting model behavior.
icml-2026-distributionally-robust-reinfo.tldr: Distributionally robust versions of RLHF and DPO improve tested performance when deployment tasks differ from the preference-training data.

paragraphs: Professional workflows require an agent to coordinate many actions while respecting permissions and tracking changes that persist. EnterpriseOps-Gym evaluates these demands in an interconnected enterprise environment. It targets the gap between answering questions or completing isolated tool calls and reliably carrying out a longer workplace process.

The benchmark includes 1,150 expert-curated tasks across eight domains, including human resources, IT, customer service, and productivity tools. Its containerized sandbox contains 164 database tables and 512 working tools. Tasks use persistent state and outcome-based verification, so evaluation concerns the resulting system state as well as the agent’s ability to plan and use tools under access constraints.

The strongest evaluated model, Claude Sonnet 4.5, succeeds on 34.1% of tasks. Reported weaknesses include inconsistent planning, poor recovery from errors, and difficulty following policy constraints. Agents also frequently attempt infeasible requests instead of refusing them, sometimes causing unintended and potentially harmful changes. The authors interpret these findings as evidence that current agents are not ready for enterprise deployment and offer the benchmark to support reliability research.
icml-2026-enterpriseops-gym-environments.tldr: EnterpriseOps-Gym tests realistic workplace agents and finds major weaknesses in planning, recovery, policy compliance, and refusal of infeasible tasks.

paragraphs: Evaluating a candidate design can be expensive, making it important to learn from each experiment. Standard black-box optimization treats the result as a single score. This paper studies a richer setting in which an experiment also produces a high-dimensional collection of auxiliary information, and previously solved related tasks are available.

The proposed method uses a neural model to predict the objective value of unseen designs from a small context of observations that includes this auxiliary information. Its central move is to use more of what an experiment reveals when forecasting which designs will perform well. The setting also incorporates relevant task history to accelerate optimization, connecting few-shot prediction with the search for better designs.

Experiments address robotic hardware design and hyperparameter tuning. In both domains, the method improves prediction from a few examples and speeds up design optimization relative to several multi-task optimization approaches. These findings support the value of auxiliary experimental outputs in the studied setting, where both rich observations and a history of related solved tasks are available.
icml-2026-few-shot-design-optimization-b.tldr: Using rich experimental outputs alongside related task history improves few-shot prediction and accelerates optimization in two design domains.

paragraphs: FrontierCS evaluates computer-science problem solving where the best possible solution is unknown but candidate solutions can still be scored objectively. Models must implement executable programs, making solution quality measurable through what their code accomplishes. This permits evaluation of progress on open-ended problems without requiring a known optimum.

The benchmark contains 240 problems designed and reviewed by experts, including computer-science PhDs and experienced competitive programmers and problem setters. It covers algorithmic challenges, often NP-hard variants of programming problems, and research problems with objective partial scoring. Each task includes an expert reference solution and an automatic evaluator, providing both a comparison point and a repeatable assessment procedure.

The experiments find a large gap between frontier reasoning models and human experts, which simply increasing reasoning budgets does not close. Models also struggle to recognize internal equivalence classes, while existing agent frameworks show brittleness attributed to overfitting. Together, these observations suggest that open-ended, graded programming challenges expose weaknesses that are not resolved merely by allocating more reasoning effort.
icml-2026-frontiercs-evolving-challenges.tldr: FrontierCS uses objectively scored, open-ended programming problems to reveal a substantial gap between frontier models and human experts.

paragraphs: A learnware market pairs trained models with specifications that help users find suitable models for new tasks without exposing their training data. The specification must describe functionality well enough to distinguish useful candidates. Existing Reduced Kernel Mean Embedding specifications summarize input distributions, which can make models look similar even when they produce different outputs.

Reduced Neural Conditional Mean Embedding, or RNCME, instead directly represents the conditional relationship between inputs and outputs. It uses Conditional Mean Embedding as its theoretical foundation. This changes the focus of a specification from the kinds of inputs associated with a model to how outputs depend on those inputs, addressing the ambiguity created by input-only descriptions.

The method applies to both classification and regression. This broadens its scope relative to the labeled-RKME improvements discussed in the paper, which are limited to classification and model the conditional relationship indirectly. The authors provide a theoretical account grounded in conditional embeddings and report empirical evidence of effectiveness and efficiency. The contribution is a more function-sensitive way to identify reusable models.
icml-2026-identifying-learnwares-via-red.tldr: RNCME describes reusable models through their input–output relationships, helping distinguish functionality across both classification and regression tasks.

paragraphs: LIFT addresses long-input understanding by adapting a language model’s parameters to each input. A short-context model can then answer questions using information absorbed during fine-tuning, even when that information is absent from the context provided at inference. The framework offers a way to handle long inputs through parameter updates.

The training process goes beyond continuing ordinary pretraining on the input text. LIFT uses specially designed synthetic tasks generated by a language model to promote comprehension beyond memorization. This is central to the approach: storing information in parameters must support answering questions about it, rather than merely retaining pieces of the original text.

The authors state that this approach avoids the quadratic input-length complexity of standard long-context models, while introducing fine-tuning overhead of its own. An optimized pipeline reduces time to the first output token to under ten seconds for an 8,000-token context. The paper also examines deployment feasibility and the framework’s strengths and limitations. Its contribution connects per-input learning with an implementation designed to make that adaptation more practical.
icml-2026-lift-a-novel-framework-for-enh.tldr: LIFT fine-tunes short-context models on each long input, using synthetic tasks to make its information available through model parameters.

paragraphs: Materials discovery involves repeatedly proposing candidates, evaluating them, and deciding what to try next. MADE evaluates that entire process. It addresses a gap in benchmarks centered on static predictions or separate computational tasks, which do not capture how a discovery system adapts its search as evidence accumulates.

The framework simulates discovery campaigns with a limited budget for oracle evaluations. The objective is to find thermodynamically stable compounds relative to a specified convex hull, making the stability reference part of the task definition. Discovery systems can be assembled from interchangeable generators, filters, and planners. This supports comparisons between fixed pipelines and agents that change their decisions during a campaign.

The authors compare efficacy and efficiency against baseline algorithms across diverse systems and methods. Their experiments find that adaptive planning becomes more important for discovery efficiency as the search space grows. The finding emphasizes the value of choosing subsequent evaluations in response to earlier results. MADE provides a common setting for studying that sequential decision process under explicit resource constraints.
icml-2026-made-benchmark-environments-fo.tldr: MADE benchmarks iterative materials discovery under limited evaluation budgets and finds adaptive planning increasingly valuable as search spaces grow.

paragraphs: Prediction-Powered Inference combines reliable labels with potentially noisy pseudo-labels to estimate statistical quantities. Earlier theory showed that the adaptive PPI++ method has asymptotic variance no worse than using reliable labels alone, regardless of pseudo-label quality. This paper asks what happens with an actual finite number of labeled examples.

For mean estimation, the authors derive exact finite-sample errors and identify settings where PPI++ performs worse than the reliable-label-only estimator. In the analyzed setting, improvement occurs if and only if pseudo-labels and reliable labels have sufficiently high correlation, with the threshold depending on the labeled sample count. For Gaussian data, the stated requirement is correlation of at least one divided by the square root of n minus two.

The paper also provides exact finite-sample variance expressions under sample splitting and illustrates its theoretical findings on real datasets. The practical message is that an asymptotic advantage does not automatically imply an advantage at a given sample size. Pseudo-label quality and available labeled data jointly determine whether the method helps in the settings analyzed.
icml-2026-no-free-lunch-non-asymptotic-a.tldr: Finite-sample analysis shows that PPI++ can worsen mean estimation unless pseudo-label correlation is high enough for the available labeled sample size.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning for language models depends on rewards that may be inconsistent or wrong. Such errors can distort the training signal, including when optimization compares groups of generated responses. This paper studies how reward noise interacts with GRPO and Dr.GRPO and develops corrections for both methods.

The framework explicitly models reward corruption as Bernoulli noise, meaning that reward errors are represented through probabilistic flips. It estimates flip probabilities and then corrects the learning signal to remove bias. Within this framework, the authors derive unbiased gradient estimates. Their theory also shows that group-based optimization already mitigates noise affecting individual examples, and that the proposed correction strengthens this robustness.

Experiments applying the correction with reward models show consistent improvements across mathematics and coding tasks. Reported gains reach 6.7 percentage points in math accuracy and 1.5 points in code accuracy under realistic reward-model conditions. The work connects techniques for correcting noisy labels in supervised learning to policy optimization, offering both an account of existing group-level robustness and a method for improving it.
icml-2026-noise-corrected-grpo-from-nois.tldr: Correcting estimated reward-flip noise gives GRPO and Dr.GRPO unbiased gradients within the proposed framework and improves tested math and code accuracy.

paragraphs: An application that chains language-model calls and tools must deal with uncertainty at multiple stages. An inaccurate intermediate answer can affect later outputs, while the application may provide no clear indication of confidence. PPDL addresses this problem by introducing a probabilistic programming language for describing these flows.

The language lets developers quantify uncertainty and carry it through the application’s sequence of operations. It also supports experimenting with different inference scaling techniques without adding code beyond the flow’s own logic. This makes the workflow description the basis for both executing the application and exploring ways to handle its uncertain results, reducing the extra implementation needed for those experiments.

The paper presents an experimental study demonstrating this capability and a case study involving a theorem-proving agent for Rocq. The case study places the programming approach in a concrete agent application that combines multiple operations. The contribution is a framework for making uncertainty part of an LLM application’s execution model, together with demonstrations of how that framework can support inference experiments and agent construction.
icml-2026-ppdl-llm-based-flows-as-probab.tldr: PPDL represents language-model workflows as probabilistic programs that propagate uncertainty and support inference-scaling experiments from the same flow logic.

paragraphs: Preference-based reinforcement learning trains an agent from comparisons between complete trajectories rather than numerical rewards. Its theory must account for both the outcomes of those trajectories and the comparative form of the feedback. This paper develops a general analysis that explicitly incorporates both aspects under a broad function-approximation framework.

The authors introduce Recursive Trajectory-based Preference Q-Learning and prove a regret guarantee growing with the square root of the interaction count. Regret measures accumulated performance shortfall, so this growth rate implies a declining average shortfall as interactions increase within the analyzed framework. A new complexity measure, Dual Episodic Eluder Dimension, describes the intrinsic difficulty of learning from these preferences.

For linear Markov decision processes, the complexity measure scales with representation dimension and episode horizon. The resulting regret bound is near-optimal relative to standard reward-based linear settings up to horizon-dependent and problem-dependent factors. The framework also recovers the best-known bounds for dueling bandits and standard outcome-based reinforcement learning, connecting these special cases to a broader account of preference learning.
icml-2026-rethinking-the-hardness-of-pbr.tldr: RTPQ achieves a square-root regret guarantee for preference-based reinforcement learning under broad function approximation, with a new measure of problem difficulty.

paragraphs: A language model can change how it answers when generation begins with carefully chosen tokens. This paper studies that behavioral flexibility by selecting prefixes from responses that exhibit a desired behavior. Conditioning on those prefixes can switch modes, such as moving between step-by-step reasoning and direct answers, without retraining the model.

The authors then introduce Token-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning, or ToCoRL, to make these temporary adaptations into stable learned behaviors. Token-conditioned generation guides exploration during reinforcement learning, while training strengthens the resulting behavioral patterns. The approach uses an inference-time capability as a starting point for learning more persistent control over how the model responds.

Experiments report precise behavioral control without capability degradation. A highlighted result concerns large reasoning models that perform strongly on complex mathematics: ToCoRL adapts them to excel at factual question answering, where their step-by-step response patterns had hindered performance. These findings suggest that, in the tested models, improving task suitability can involve changing the expression of existing capabilities through behavioral adaptation.
icml-2026-revealing-behavioral-plasticit.tldr: ToCoRL turns behavior changes elicited by selected token prefixes into stable learned response patterns without capability degradation in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Understanding how visual concepts emerge inside a deep model requires ways to characterize its internal features. SAEs-BrainMap uses human brain activity as an external reference for this task. It focuses on activation patterns from the ventral visual pathway to guide the identification of features extracted by sparse autoencoders.

The framework aligns sparse model features with biological regions of interest. The authors report robust representational alignment through both quantitative and qualitative analyses. This supports the feasibility of using brain signals to characterize model functionality: the measured relationships provide evidence for interpreting what particular model features represent.

The authors then use this alignment to follow generic concepts across model layers and visualize the model’s overall processing flow using the brain’s hierarchical organization. The contribution therefore extends from interpreting individual features to tracing how representations develop through the network. Its stated findings concern representational correspondence and interpretability, providing an empirical basis for connecting sparse feature analysis with a biologically organized view of visual processing.
icml-2026-saes-brainmap-unveiling-the-em.tldr: SAEs-BrainMap aligns sparse model features with visual brain responses to interpret concepts and trace their progression across network layers.

paragraphs: Images contain more visual detail than short captions typically describe. The paper argues that this imbalance can cause image–text alignment systems to suppress useful image regions or associate concepts ambiguously. Adding richer descriptions from multimodal language models can help, but inconsistencies with the original captions can also shift the intended meaning.

SEPS addresses this through a calibration mechanism that combines an overall visual-language description from a multimodal model with the original sparse query. Patch selection becomes a process of finding agreement between detailed local distinctions and the broader image context. This is intended to retain image regions that are informative without losing the meaning established by the query.

A second component emphasizes salient patch–word matches when combining similarity scores. It addresses the dilution that can occur when strong local matches are averaged together with less relevant information. Experiments on Flickr30K and MS-COCO report significant text-to-image retrieval gains over existing state-of-the-art approaches across multiple backbones. The results support combining calibrated descriptions, selective visual patches, and relevance-sensitive aggregation.
icml-2026-seps-semantic-enhanced-patch-s.tldr: SEPS calibrates richer image descriptions against sparse queries and emphasizes salient local matches to improve text-to-image retrieval.

paragraphs: Text watermark detectors can lose accuracy when passages are short or repeatedly paraphrased. Pattern Stability Score addresses this by examining local statistical patterns and how those patterns behave across successive paraphrases. The aim is to identify watermark evidence that remains useful after the wording has changed.

The framework combines global and local z-scores with statistics describing runs of patterns, autocorrelation signals, and stability measurements across paraphrase depth. These features bring together overall evidence, local structure, and persistence under rewriting. The evaluation uses three datasets, multiple generation models and paraphrasers, and as many as eight rounds of paraphrasing to stress-test detection.

Compared with z-score thresholding baselines and some deep-learning methods, the authors report AUC gains exceeding 10–15 percentage points across different text lengths. A single classifier also transfers across tested language models, paraphrasers, and domains without retraining. It maintains above 83.7% AUC when all those components differ from training, supporting the value of stability-aware features for watermark detection under the evaluated shifts.
icml-2026-stability-aware-feature-design.tldr: Pattern Stability Score improves watermark detection by combining local text statistics with their stability across repeated paraphrasing.

paragraphs: Some graphs are defined through functions of node features rather than an explicitly stored collection of edges. SWING develops algorithms for Graph Random Feature computations on these implicit graphs. The setting includes epsilon-neighborhood graphs, where connections are determined by relationships between points in a feature space.

The key change is to conduct walks in the continuous space containing the graph instead of walking directly between graph nodes. To approximate the original graph computations accurately and efficiently, SWING combines a customized Gumbel-softmax sampling mechanism with kernels linearized through random features and importance sampling. The construction uses a connection between implicit graph representations and Fourier analysis developed in the paper.

SWING is designed to work well on accelerators and does not require materializing the input graph. This matters because the computation can use the feature-based representation directly rather than first constructing all graph connections. The paper supplies detailed analysis and experiments across different classes of implicit graphs, supporting the proposed route from continuous-space sampling to approximate combinatorial graph calculations.
icml-2026-swing-unlocking-implicit-graph.tldr: SWING approximates Graph Random Feature computations through continuous-space walks, avoiding explicit construction of feature-defined graphs.

paragraphs: Generating an image containing substantial text requires handling the words, their arrangement, and their meaning together. Existing datasets mainly emphasize short, simple text. TextAtlas5M broadens the target to include longer passages, more complex layouts, and richer semantic content, treating these as interconnected aspects of dense-text image generation.

The dataset contains five million generated and collected images covering diverse data types. The authors also create TextAtlasEval, a set of 4,000 human-improved test cases spanning four domains. Together, the training resource and evaluation set support studying text-rich image generation at scale while assessing more demanding cases than simple short-text rendering.

Evaluations find substantial challenges even for state-of-the-art proprietary models such as GPT-4o, with larger performance gaps for open-source models. Training on TextAtlas5M consistently improves text rendering for both diffusion and autoregressive models in the reported experiments. The contribution therefore supplies both a demanding evaluation resource and training data that demonstrably helps two different families of image generators.
icml-2026-textatlas5m-a-large-scale-data.tldr: TextAtlas5M supplies five million images for dense-text generation and improves rendering in tested diffusion and autoregressive models.

paragraphs: Agents that evaluate their own outputs depend on a model applying relevant concepts similarly when producing and reviewing an answer. This paper measures that assumption directly through generator–evaluator self-consistency. The measure concerns agreement between two roles played by the same model, which matters when a workflow lacks external verification.

The authors assess ten frontier models across 491 concepts and find substantial differences in self-consistency. They then examine a clinical setting containing physician-validated mistakes. Across models, greater self-consistency is associated with greater vulnerability to those mistakes. The reported relationship is an association across the evaluated models, rather than evidence that increasing consistency itself causes errors.

The resulting dilemma is that consistency can help a workflow operate coherently while still failing to establish that its decisions are safe. A model can apply concepts consistently during generation and evaluation yet remain vulnerable to mistakes. The findings challenge the use of self-agreement as a sufficient basis for trusting self-evaluating agents, particularly in the clinical setting studied.
icml-2026-the-consistency-dilemma-in-llm.tldr: Models vary in generation–evaluation consistency, and higher consistency is associated with greater mistake vulnerability in the studied clinical setting.

paragraphs: Long reasoning sequences create large key–value caches, making memory a bottleneck during generation. Compression methods must decide which stored keys remain important. This paper argues that estimating importance from recent queries after rotary position encoding can be unreliable because those queries rotate with position and provide too few representative samples.

The authors instead examine queries and keys before positional rotation. They observe that these vectors concentrate around stable, nonzero centers. Their analysis connects those centers to preferences for keys at particular distances through a trigonometric series. TriAttention uses the resulting positional preferences, together with query and key norms, to estimate which keys should be retained.

On AIME25 with generation lengths of 32,000 tokens, TriAttention matches full-attention reasoning accuracy while providing either 2.5 times higher throughput or a 10.7-fold reduction in key–value memory. Leading comparison methods achieve about half the accuracy at the same efficiency. These results support using the observed pre-rotation structure to compress memory while preserving long-reasoning performance in the evaluated setting.
icml-2026-triattention-efficient-long-re.tldr: TriAttention uses stable query–key structure before positional rotation to compress caches while matching full-attention accuracy on the reported long-reasoning evaluation.

paragraphs: Dynamic 3D generation must keep a scene coherent across time and viewpoints. The spatio-camera-motion attention used to maintain this consistency can require substantial computation and memory, causing long generation times and out-of-memory failures. Turbo4DGen targets this bottleneck in diffusion-based generation of dynamic scenes from multiple views.

The framework combines three ways to reduce repeated attention work. A spatiotemporal cache reuses intermediate attention across denoising steps. Semantic-aware pruning dynamically reduces attention computation, while an adaptive scheduler bypasses parts of the spatio-camera-motion chain. Together, these mechanisms target redundant computation within the process responsible for maintaining spatial, temporal, and viewpoint consistency.

Experiments on ObjaverseDy and Consistent4D report an average 9.7-fold speedup without quality degradation. This is an empirical result on the evaluated datasets, showing that substantial acceleration is possible while preserving the measured generation quality. The contribution is a dedicated acceleration framework that coordinates reuse, pruning, and scheduling around the attention demands specific to dynamic, multi-view 3D content generation.
icml-2026-turbo4dgen-ultra-fast-accelera.tldr: Turbo4DGen reduces redundant attention work and achieves an average 9.7-fold generation speedup without quality degradation on two evaluated datasets.

paragraphs: Flow maps can generate high-quality images in one forward pass, but this speed removes the explicit sequence of sampling steps commonly used to guide generation toward an observation. Variational Flow Maps address conditional generation by adapting the initial noise supplied to the generator. The observation influences where generation starts.

Given an observation, a noise adapter predicts a distribution of starting noise whose mapped outputs should respect both the observation and the learned data prior. A variational objective jointly trains the adapter and flow map to improve the alignment between noise and data. This joint training is intended to let a simple adapter support sampling from a complex conditional distribution.

Across several inverse problems, the authors report well-calibrated conditional samples produced in one or a few steps. On ImageNet, the method achieves competitive fidelity while accelerating sampling by orders of magnitude relative to alternative iterative diffusion and flow models. These findings support learning the conditioning in the initial noise distribution as a practical route to fast conditional generation.
icml-2026-variational-flow-maps-make-som.tldr: Variational Flow Maps learn observation-dependent starting noise to produce well-calibrated conditional samples in one or a few generation steps.
